order.why_here: The simplest heap use: a size-k min-heap whose root is the k-th largest.
Same question on static data; quickselect shows when a heap is not the best tool.
Size-k club again, but the bouncer is the farthest point, so the heap becomes a max-heap by negation.
Size-k club with a two-key ordering that includes a string, forcing a custom comparison.
The heap turns from a filter into a greedy chooser, paired with a cooldown queue.
Same most-frequent-first greedy with a cooldown of one and a counting feasibility test.
Generalises the one-slot parking spot to a fixed-length cooldown queue of k.
Introduces the k-way merge: one front item per sorted source in a min-heap.
k-way merge over implicit sorted rows that are generated, never stored.
k-way merge plus a running maximum tracked beside the heap.
k-way merge embedded in a design problem, keyed by time stamps.
Two balanced heaps facing each other expose the middle of a stream.
Sort by threshold, unlock into a max-heap, and pop the best each time you commit.
Unlock-then-choose, but commit retroactively only when stuck.
Sort by deadline and keep a max-heap of chosen items so the worst can be swapped out.
Sort by the bottleneck and keep the best k other values in a size-k min-heap.
Normalise to a single direction of moves, then repeatedly shrink the heap maximum.
Two heaps (free rooms by id, busy rooms by end time) driven by a time-sorted sweep.
Sweep-line events with a max-heap of heights and lazy deletion.
A min-heap frontier growing inward from the border: Dijkstra's shape on a grid.
